warmup.q:
What does firstDeclined(listOf("APPROVED p1", "DECLINED p2", "APPROVED p3")) return?

fun firstDeclined(results: List<String>): String? {
    results.forEach { if (it.startsWith("DECLINED")) return it }
    return null
}
options: null, because return only leaves the lambda and forEach carries on
It doesn't compile: return is not allowed inside a lambda
It throws, because forEach can't be stopped early
warmup.why: forEach is an inline function, so its lambda is pasted into firstDeclined, and a bare return there returns from firstDeclined itself. That's a non-local return. In Java, return inside a forEach lambda would only leave the lambda, which is why the first option is tempting. Inside a lambda passed to an ordinary function, the third option would be right.

sections.h: inline pastes the function and its lambda into the caller
sections.html:
Every lambda you pass to an ordinary function is an object. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: each function is an object, it captures a closure, and the memory allocations and virtual calls cost something at run time. inline removes that object. The compiler copies the function's body, and the body of the lambda you passed, into every place that calls it.

Here is a timing helper in both languages:

Java
// Java has no inline: the helper always receives a real Supplier object
static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) {
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    try {
        return block.get();
    } finally {
        System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us");
    }
}

long fee = timed("fee", () -> amountMinor * 3 / 100);
Kotlin
inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T {
    val start = System.nanoTime()
    try {
        return block()
    } finally {
        println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us")
    }
}

fun feeInline(amountMinor: Long): Long = timed("inline") { amountMinor * 3 / 100 }

The demo below has a second copy, timedNotInline, that differs only by the missing keyword. javap shows what each caller turned into. The ordinary call site is seven instructions long: invokedynamic builds a Function0, invokestatic calls timedNotInline with it, and checkcast java/lang/Number plus longValue unbox the generic result. The inline call site has none of that. The multiply (lmul, ldiv) sits right inside feeInline, between two calls to System.nanoTime.

Read a bit further and you see the price. The finally block appears twice in feeInline, once for the normal exit and once for the exit by exception. That is real code growth, repeated in every caller. The docs warn that inlining "may cause the generated code to grow" and say it pays off if you avoid inlining large functions.

So inline is for small functions that take lambdas. The standard library is full of them: forEach, map, filter, let, apply, use, repeat, synchronized, require. Because they are inline, payments.map { it.amountMinor } costs about what a hand-written loop costs. The generics track used inline for one more reason: a reified type parameter exists only because the body is copied to a call site where the type is known.

Java gets none of this. javac can't inline Kotlin code, so for Java InlineDemoKt.timed(...) is an ordinary static method that takes a Function0, and the Java lambda becomes an object like any other.

try.title: Read the bytecode of an inline call
steps: Run InlineDemo (or InlineDemoJava) with the command below. Both print fee = 360.
Find feeNotInline and feeInline. Before you look, predict which one contains invokedynamic and which one contains lmul. Then count the println calls inside feeInline.

code.title: InlineDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo /** inline: the compiler pastes this body, and the lambda's body, into every caller. */ inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } /** The same function without inline: the caller builds a Function0 object and calls through it. */ fun <T> timedNotInline(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } fun feeInline(amountMinor: Long): Long = timed("inline") { amountMinor * 3 / 100 } fun feeNotInline(amountMinor: Long): Long = timedNotInline("not inline") { amountMinor * 3 / 100 } fun main() { println("fee = ${feeInline(12_000)}") println("fee = ${feeNotInline(12_000)}") }

alt.title: InlineDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; /** * Java twin of InlineDemo.kt. javac cannot inline Kotlin code, so for Java the inline function * timed() is an ordinary static method on InlineDemoKt that takes a Function0. */ public class InlineDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { // the Java lambda becomes a Function0 object; timed() calls its invoke() like any other method long fee = InlineDemoKt.timed("from Java", () -> 12_000L * 3 / 100); System.out.println("fee = " + fee); // the same idea written in plain Java: a Supplier and a call through it long same = timedJava("plain Java", () -> 12_000L * 3 / 100); System.out.println("fee = " + same); } static <T> T timedJava(String label, java.util.function.Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } }

try.expect: feeNotInline is short: invokedynamic (a new Function0), invokestatic timedNotInline, then checkcast java/lang/Number and longValue to unbox the result. feeInline holds the arithmetic (lmul, ldiv) and two PrintStream.println calls, because the finally block was copied for both exits. Ignore the microsecond timings: one cold call measures class loading and lambda setup, not inlining. The bytecode is the evidence.

sections.h: A bare return in an inlined lambda leaves the caller
sections.html:
Inside an ordinary lambda, a bare return doesn't compile. The error is 'return' is prohibited here. A lambda is an object with its own method, and that method can't make some other function return. An inlined lambda is different. Its body becomes part of the caller, so return can mean exactly what it says.

Java
static String firstDeclined(List<String> results) {
    for (String r : results) {
        if (r.startsWith("DECLINED")) return r;     // Java needs a real loop to return early
    }
    return null;
}

static int countApproved(List<String> results) {
    int approved = 0;
    for (String r : results) {
        if (!r.startsWith("APPROVED")) continue;
        approved++;
    }
    return approved;
}
Kotlin
fun firstDeclined(results: List<String>): String? {
    results.forEach { if (it.startsWith("DECLINED")) return it }   // leaves firstDeclined
    return null
}

fun countApproved(results: List<String>): Int {
    var approved = 0
    results.forEach {
        if (!it.startsWith("APPROVED")) return@forEach              // leaves this lambda call only
        approved++
    }
    return approved
}

The first return is a non-local return: it leaves the function that contains the lambda. It compiles only because forEach is inline. In the bytecode, firstDeclined is an Iterator loop with an areturn in the middle, and no lambda object exists at all.

To leave only the current call of the lambda, add a label. return@forEach behaves like continue in a loop.

Since Kotlin 2.2.0, break and continue also work inside a lambda passed to an inline function. The feature is stable, so you need no compiler flag. In the demo, break inside batch.forEach { } leaves the outer for loop, the way Java's labeled break outer does.

Java has no non-local return. A Java lambda always compiles to a separate method, so return inside forEach(r -> { ... }) only ends that one call and the loop goes on. The demo's firstDeclinedBroken shows it: it always returns null. People who move from Java to Kotlin make the opposite mistake. They write return inside forEach to skip one element, and the whole function exits instead.

try.title: Return, label, break
steps: Run NonLocalReturnDemo and then NonLocalReturnDemoJava. Before you run the Java one, predict what firstDeclinedBroken prints.
Work out totalUntilVoid by hand from the three batches in main, then check your number against the output.
Uncomment the wrong move at the bottom of main (a lambda stored in a val). Predict the error, run, then comment it out again.

code.title: NonLocalReturnDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo /** A bare `return` inside forEach's lambda returns from firstDeclined: forEach is inline. */ fun firstDeclined(results: List<String>): String? { results.forEach { if (it.startsWith("DECLINED")) return it } return null } /** `return@forEach` leaves only the current lambda call, like `continue` in a loop. */ fun countApproved(results: List<String>): Int { var approved = 0 results.forEach { if (!it.startsWith("APPROVED")) return@forEach approved++ } return approved } /** Since Kotlin 2.2, `break` and `continue` work inside an inlined lambda too. */ fun totalUntilVoid(batches: List<List<Long>>): Long { var total = 0L for (batch in batches) { batch.forEach { amount -> if (amount < 0) break // leaves the for loop, not just the lambda total += amount } } return total } fun main() { val results = listOf("APPROVED pay_1", "DECLINED pay_2 insufficient funds", "APPROVED pay_3") println("firstDeclined = ${firstDeclined(results)}") println("countApproved = ${countApproved(results)}") println("totalUntilVoid = ${totalUntilVoid(listOf(listOf(1_000L, 250L), listOf(400L, -1L, 900L), listOf(75L)))}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val lookup = { r: String -> if (r.isEmpty()) return; r.length } }

alt.title: NonLocalReturnDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of NonLocalReturnDemo.kt. A Java lambda is always a separate method, so `return` * inside it only leaves the lambda. To return from the enclosing method you need a real loop. */ public class NonLocalReturnDemoJava { static String firstDeclined(List<String> results) { for (String r : results) { if (r.startsWith("DECLINED")) return r; // a loop, so return leaves the method } return null; } static String firstDeclinedBroken(List<String> results) { results.forEach(r -> { if (r.startsWith("DECLINED")) return; // leaves this lambda call only }); return null; // always reached } static long totalUntilVoid(List<List<Long>> batches) { long total = 0; outer: for (List<Long> batch : batches) { for (long amount : batch) { if (amount < 0) break outer; // Java's labeled break: Kotlin's non-local break total += amount; } } return total; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> results = List.of("APPROVED pay_1", "DECLINED pay_2 insufficient funds", "APPROVED pay_3"); System.out.println("firstDeclined = " + firstDeclined(results)); System.out.println("firstDeclinedBroken = " + firstDeclinedBroken(results)); System.out.println("totalUntilVoid = " + totalUntilVoid(List.of(List.of(1_000L, 250L), List.of(400L, -1L, 900L), List.of(75L)))); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints firstDeclined = DECLINED pay_2 insufficient funds, countApproved = 2 and totalUntilVoid = 1650 (1,000 + 250 + 400, then the -1 breaks out of the outer loop, so 900 and 75 are never added). Java's firstDeclinedBroken prints null. The wrong move fails with 'return' is prohibited here. (Gradle adds RETURN_NOT_ALLOWED): a lambda stored in a val is an object, so it can't return from main.

sections.h: When a lambda can't be pasted: noinline and crossinline
sections.html:
Inlining works only if the compiler can paste the lambda's body where you call it. Two things get in the way, and each one has its own modifier.

The first is using the lambda as a value. An inlined lambda has no object behind it, so you can't store it in a field, add it to a list or pass it to an ordinary function. Try it and the compiler says illegal usage of inline parameter 'listener: (String) -> Unit'. Add 'noinline' modifier to the parameter declaration. noinline turns that one parameter back into a normal lambda object. The other parameters are still inlined.

The second is calling the lambda from somewhere else: inside an object, a Runnable or another lambda. The docs call this "another execution context". That code runs later, maybe on another thread, when the caller may have returned long ago. A non-local return from there can't work, so the compiler stops you: cannot inline 'task: () -> Unit' here: it might contain non-local returns. Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'task: () -> Unit'.

crossinline is a rule for the caller's lambda: no bare return inside it. With that rule in place, the compiler still pastes the lambda's body, now into a Runnable class it generates for that call site. In the demo, javap finds a class called ModifiersDemoKt$main$$inlined$runInBackground$1 with no Function0 field: the body of the caller's lambda is inside its run().

Java
// Java lambdas already behave like crossinline ones: return leaves only the lambda
static void runInBackground(Executor executor, Runnable task) {
    executor.execute(task);
}

runInBackground(pool, () -> System.out.println("settling batch 17"));
Kotlin
inline fun runInBackground(executor: Executor, crossinline task: () -> Unit) {
    executor.execute { task() }          // task runs later, on a pool thread
}

runInBackground(pool) { println("settling batch 17") }
// runInBackground(pool) { return }     // error: 'return' is prohibited here.

Both modifiers would make that function compile, so pick by what you do with the lambda. Use crossinline when you call it inside another lambda or object, because its body is still inlined into the new class. Use noinline when the lambda has to exist as a value you keep or hand on. Neither modifier changes the JVM signature: Java sees a Function0 either way.

You'll need crossinline all the time at work. Plenty of Java APIs take a callback: Executor.execute(Runnable), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(Supplier), a transaction template's execute(callback), Temporal's Async.function(...). Every inline Kotlin wrapper around one of them needs it.

try.title: Make the compiler ask for each modifier
steps: Run ModifiersDemo (or ModifiersDemoJava, which calls the same Kotlin functions with plain Java lambdas).
In ModifiersDemo.kt, delete noinline in subscribe. Predict the error, run, read it, then put it back.
Delete crossinline in runInBackground, run, and put it back.
Uncomment the last line of main and run. Why does the compiler refuse a return that it allowed in forEach?

code.title: ModifiersDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.Executor import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit val listeners = mutableListOf<(String) -> Unit>() /** noinline: `listener` is stored in a list, so it has to stay a real object. `log` is inlined. */ inline fun subscribe(log: (String) -> Unit, noinline listener: (String) -> Unit) { log("subscribing listener #${listeners.size + 1}") listeners += listener } /** crossinline: `task` runs inside a Runnable on another thread, so it may not return from the caller. */ inline fun runInBackground(executor: Executor, crossinline task: () -> Unit) { executor.execute { task() } } fun main() { subscribe({ println(it) }) { event -> println("listener got $event") } listeners.forEach { it("payment-captured") } val pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { Thread(it, "settlement-worker") } runInBackground(pool) { println("running on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Wrong moves, one at a time. Predict the error, run, then undo. // 1. Delete `noinline` in subscribe. // 2. Delete `crossinline` in runInBackground. // 3. Uncomment the next line. // runInBackground(pool) { return } }

Every Java lambda already behaves like a * crossinline one, because `return` in a Java lambda can only leave the lambda. */ public class ModifiersDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { // subscribe(Function1<? super String, Unit>, Function1<? super String, Unit>) ModifiersDemoKt.subscribe( line -> { System.out.println(line); return Unit.INSTANCE; }, event -> { System.out.println("listener got " + event); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); ModifiersDemoKt.getListeners().forEach(l -> l.invoke("payment-captured")); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "settlement-worker")); // runInBackground(Executor, Function0<Unit>) ModifiersDemoKt.runInBackground(pool, () -> { System.out.println("running on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

Without noinline the build fails with illegal usage of inline parameter 'listener: (String) -> Unit'. Without crossinline it fails with cannot inline 'task: () -> Unit' here: it might contain non-local returns. The last line fails with 'return' is prohibited here.: by the time the Runnable runs on the pool thread, main may be somewhere else entirely.

sections.html:
inline has costs, and three of them show up in real code.

The first is size. The body is copied into every caller, so a 40-line function called from 200 places becomes 200 copies. The compiler even warns when you inline a function that takes no lambdas: expected performance impact from inlining is insignificant. Inlining works best for functions with parameters of function types. The JIT already inlines small, hot methods at run time (the performance track covers how), so a lambda-free inline fun buys you nothing.

The second is frozen bodies. A caller gets its copy of the body when the caller is compiled. In one test run, a client was compiled against version 1 of a small library, and then version 2 replaced the library jar without recompiling the client. The client printed inline=v1 plain=v2: the ordinary function ran the new code, and the inline one still ran the old copy. So if you publish a shared library, such as an internal payments SDK, treat a public inline body like a public signature. Changing it takes effect only when every client is rebuilt.

The third is visibility, and it follows from the second. The body lands in other modules, so it may only use what those modules could use. Call a private function from a public inline one and you get public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function. The fix is @PublishedApi internal: still hidden from Kotlin callers, but public in the bytecode, so the pasted copies can reach it. The helper's own body is not copied anywhere, so it can use private state freely.

Java
// Java has no internal or inline. The nearest shape: one public helper that callers reach
public final class Tracing {
    private static final AtomicInteger COUNTER = new AtomicInteger();
    public static String nextTraceId() { return "trace-" + COUNTER.incrementAndGet(); }
}
Kotlin
inline fun <T> traced(operation: String, block: () -> T): T {
    val id = nextTraceId()                  // must be reachable from every caller's module
    println("[$id] start $operation")
    val result = block()
    println("[$id] end $operation")
    return result
}

@PublishedApi
internal fun nextTraceId(): String = "trace-" + counter.incrementAndGet()

private val counter = AtomicInteger()       // fine: nextTraceId is not inline

The compiler adds two hard limits. An inline function can't call itself (inline function 'fun recI(n: Int): Int' cannot be recursive.), and it can't contain a local function (local functions are not yet supported in inline functions.).

Properties can be inline too, as long as the accessor has no backing field: val Long.asEuros: String inline get() = .... You'll mostly see that for a property with a reified type parameter.

Here's my rule. Inline small functions that take lambdas, or that need reified or a non-local return. Leave everything else ordinary. If the inline body starts to grow, keep the inline part to a few lines and move the real work into a @PublishedApi internal function, which is compiled once.

try.title: Break the visibility rule
steps: In PublishedApiDemo.kt, change @PublishedApi internal fun nextTraceId() to private fun nextTraceId(). Predict the error and run the Kotlin demo.
Put it back. Why can the Java twin call nextTraceId() directly, when Kotlin code in another module could not?

code.title: PublishedApiDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** * A public inline function is pasted into callers, possibly in another module. So its body may * only use declarations those callers could use themselves. */ inline fun <T> traced(operation: String, block: () -> T): T { val id = nextTraceId() println("[$id] start $operation") val result = block() println("[$id] end $operation") return result } /** Not part of the Kotlin API, but public in the bytecode, so the pasted copies can call it. */ @PublishedApi internal fun nextTraceId(): String = "trace-" + counter.incrementAndGet() private val counter = AtomicInteger() // fine: nextTraceId is not inline, so its body is never copied /** An inline property: no backing field, and the getter is pasted into each caller. */ val Long.asEuros: String inline get() = "EUR " + (this / 100) + "." + (this % 100).toString().padStart(2, '0') fun main() { val refunded = traced("refund pay_7") { 1_999L } println("refunded ${refunded.asEuros}") // Wrong move. Change `@PublishedApi internal` on nextTraceId to `private`, predict, run. }

alt.title: PublishedApiDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; /** * Java twin of PublishedApiDemo.kt. `internal` is a Kotlin rule that javac does not know about. * In the bytecode nextTraceId() is public, so Java can call it, and traced() is an ordinary method. */ public class PublishedApiDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { long refunded = PublishedApiDemoKt.traced("refund pay_7", () -> 1_999L); System.out.println("refunded " + PublishedApiDemoKt.getAsEuros(refunded)); System.out.println("Java can call the internal helper too: " + PublishedApiDemoKt.nextTraceId()); } }

try.expect: Both print [trace-1] start refund pay_7, [trace-1] end refund pay_7 and refunded EUR 19.99, and the Java twin also prints trace-2 from a direct call. With private, the build fails with public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function. internal is a Kotlin rule; in the bytecode the function is public, and javac doesn't know the rule exists.

analogy: Inlining is a cook copying the recipe onto every order ticket instead of pinning one copy on the wall. Nobody walks to the wall, so each order moves faster, but every ticket gets longer. If the head chef fixes the recipe on the wall, tickets that were already printed still carry the old version: that's the frozen-body problem. The analogy breaks at crossinline. A cook can't accidentally walk out of the restaurant, but a lambda copied into a Runnable could try to return from a function that finished minutes ago, so the compiler has to forbid it.
world: Your Quarkus services are full of small wrappers: timed("issuer.authorize") { client.authorize(req) } around a metrics timer, withMdc("paymentId", id) { ... } around logging, a retry around a card-issuer call that takes 120 ms and sometimes times out. Each one is a good inline candidate: a few lines, a lambda parameter, called on every request. The moment a wrapper hands the lambda to a Java API (executor.execute, CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, a transaction callback, Temporal's Async.function), its parameter needs crossinline. And if those wrappers live in a shared library that ten services use, a fix to an inline body reaches each service only when that service is rebuilt against the new version.
mistake:
Writing return inside forEach to skip one element. In Java, return in a forEach lambda skips to the next element, and many people carry that habit into Kotlin:

Java
batch.forEach(p -> {
    if (p.amountMinor() == 0) return;     // Java: skips this payment, carries on
    ledger.post(p);
});
Kotlin
batch.forEach { p ->
    if (p.amountMinor == 0L) return       // Kotlin: leaves the whole function
    ledger.post(p)
}

In Kotlin forEach is inline, so the bare return leaves the enclosing function, and every payment after the first zero-amount one is silently skipped. It compiles without a warning. Write return@forEach to skip one element, or use a plain for loop with continue, which reads better anyway.

compare.title: Wrapping a callback API: Java Supplier vs Kotlin inline with crossinline

java.title: Timing.java
java.html: import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.Executor; import java.util.function.Supplier; final class Timing { static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } // the caller's lambda is an object; supplyAsync gets a second lambda that calls it static <T> CompletableFuture<T> timedAsync(String label, Executor executor, Supplier<T> block) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> timed(label, block), executor); } } // call site: Timing.timedAsync("capture", pool, () -> gateway.capture(authId));

kotlin.title: Timing.kt
kotlin.html: import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executor inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } // block runs inside the Supplier, another execution context: crossinline inline fun <T> timedAsync(label: String, executor: Executor, crossinline block: () -> T): CompletableFuture<T> = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ timed(label) { block() } }, executor) // call site: timedAsync("capture", pool) { gateway.capture(authId) }

compare.note: In Java the caller's lambda is always an object, and timedAsync wraps it in a second one for supplyAsync. In Kotlin the compiler pastes both timed and the caller's lambda into one Supplier class that it generates for that call site, so there is one object instead of two and no call through Supplier.get on the caller's code. The bigger difference is the rule on the caller: inside the Kotlin block a bare return is a compile error, while a Java lambda simply can't express one. Java code that calls the Kotlin timedAsync gets the ordinary compiled body and passes a Function0.

worked.title: Write an inline transaction helper over a Java callback API

steps.say: A Java library (invented for this example) runs work inside a database transaction through a callback. You want Kotlin callers to write tx.transaction { ledger.post(entry) }. Start with the API and an ordinary Kotlin wrapper.
steps.code: public interface TxRunner { <T> T inTransaction(Callable<T> work); } // Java callers write the Callable themselves long balance = tx.inTransaction(() -> ledger.balanceOf("merchant-981"));

alt.html: interface TxRunner { fun <T> inTransaction(work: Callable<T>): T } // 1. an ordinary wrapper: it works, but each call builds a Function0 and a Callable fun <T> TxRunner.transaction(block: () -> T): T = inTransaction(Callable { block() })

steps.say: The wrapper is one line and runs on every request, so make it inline. The compiler refuses, because block() is now called inside the Callable, which the library may run later or on another thread.
steps.code: // 2. add inline: the compiler stops here inline fun <T> TxRunner.transaction(block: () -> T): T = inTransaction(Callable { block() }) // error: cannot inline 'block: () -> T' here: it might contain non-local returns. // Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'block: () -> T'.

alt.html: // Java has no inline and no non-local return, so the question never comes up: // a return inside the Callable lambda only ends the Callable long posted = tx.inTransaction(() -> { ledger.post(entry); return 1L; });

steps.say: Add crossinline. The caller's lambda is now pasted into a Callable class the compiler generates for each call site. In exchange, callers lose the non-local return: that's the rule crossinline enforces.
steps.code: // 3. crossinline: inlined into the generated Callable, no bare return allowed inline fun <T> TxRunner.transaction(crossinline block: () -> T): T = inTransaction(Callable { block() }) fun post(entry: JournalEntry) { tx.transaction { ledger.post(entry) } // tx.transaction { if (entry.isEmpty) return } // error: 'return' is prohibited here. }

alt.html: void post(JournalEntry entry) { tx.inTransaction(() -> { ledger.post(entry); return null; // Callable must return something }); }

steps.say: Check that it earns its place. It does: one line, a lambda parameter, called constantly. If it later grows logging, metrics and error mapping, keep the inline part to this one line and move the rest into a @PublishedApi internal function, so 300 call sites don't each carry a copy.

lab.title: An inline retry helper, sync and async
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail with NotImplementedError. Read Callers.kt but don't edit it: the tests go through it, and its comment says why.
Write retry (TODO 1). Start at attempt 1, return block(attempt) inside a try, catch Exception, and decide whether to go round again. Keep the earlier failures in a list.
When you stop, throw giveUp(attempt, e, earlier). The build now fails. Read the error, and fix the declaration of giveUp (TODO 2), not retry.
Write retryAsync (TODO 3) as CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ retry(maxAttempts) { block(it) } }, executor). Add the modifier the compiler asks for.
Run the tests until all eight pass, including RetryFromJavaTest, which calls your retry from Java with no inlining at all.
Optional: add crossinline to retry's block and run again. Callers.firstApproved stops compiling, because its return card is a non-local return. Undo it.
hints: require(maxAttempts >= 1) { "maxAttempts must be at least 1" } throws IllegalArgumentException before the loop starts, so the block is never called.
A while (true) loop whose body ends only with return or throw needs no return after it. The compiler knows the loop never falls through.
The fix for TODO 2 is two words on the declaration: @PublishedApi internal fun giveUp(...). internal keeps it out of the Kotlin API, and @PublishedApi lets public inline bodies call it.
supplyAsync stores a thrown exception in the future, and get() reports it as an ExecutionException whose cause is your RetryExhaustedException. You don't have to write anything for that.
lab.done: All eight tests in RetryTest and RetryFromJavaTest pass.

drill.title: Write timed and timedAsync from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write an inline timed(label, block) that returns the block's result and prints the elapsed time even when the block throws. Then write timedAsync(label, executor, block) that runs timed on an executor and returns a CompletableFuture. Which parameter needs a modifier, and which one?

answer.html: inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } // block is called inside the Supplier: another execution context, so crossinline inline fun <T> timedAsync(label: String, executor: Executor, crossinline block: () -> T): CompletableFuture<T> = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ timed(label) { block() } }, executor)

alt.title: Timing.java
alt.html: static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } // no modifier exists in Java: the Supplier is always an object static <T> CompletableFuture<T> timedAsync(String label, Executor executor, Supplier<T> block) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> timed(label, block), executor); }

recap: inline copies the function body and the bodies of its lambda arguments into each caller: no Function object, no call through an interface, no boxing of a generic result.

A bare return in a lambda passed to an inline function is a non-local return and leaves the enclosing function. return@forEach leaves only the lambda. Since Kotlin 2.2, break and continue work there too.

noinline keeps one lambda as a real object you can store or pass on. crossinline lets you call a lambda from another execution context (a Runnable, a Supplier, an object) by forbidding non-local returns in it.
Inline only small functions that take lambdas. Every caller carries a copy, and a public inline body stays frozen in a client until that client is recompiled.
A public inline function may only use public API. Reach a helper through @PublishedApi internal.
Java never inlines Kotlin code. It calls the compiled body and passes Function0 or Function1 objects.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why the compiler made them write crossinline in inline fun <T> TxRunner.transaction(block: () -> T) = inTransaction(Callable { block() }). Explain, in your own words, what could go wrong without it and what they give up by adding it.
explain.answer: Because the function is inline, the caller's lambda is pasted into the caller, and normally a bare return in it would return from the caller. Here the lambda isn't called directly: it's called inside a Callable that the transaction library runs, maybe later and maybe on another thread. By then the caller's function may already have returned, so a return from inside the Callable can't mean "return from the caller". The compiler can't allow that, so it asks for crossinline. With crossinline, the compiler still pastes the lambda's body, now into a Callable class it generates for that call site, and in exchange callers may not write a bare return in the block. They can still use a labeled return like return@transaction. noinline would also compile, but it keeps the lambda as a separate object, which is the fix for storing a lambda, not for calling it somewhere else.

deeper.html:
Kotlin's inlining and the JIT's inlining are different tools. Kotlin inlines at compile time, across modules, before the JVM ever sees the code. That is the only kind that can make a non-local return or a reified type work, because both change what the code means. The JIT inlines at run time, only on hot paths, and can undo its choice (deoptimization) when its assumptions break. The lesson "Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics" in the performance track covers that side.

The Kotlin docs say inlining pays off "especially at 'megamorphic' call-sites inside loops". Here's why. An ordinary forEach taking a Function1 has one invoke call site inside it. If 30 different lambdas flow through that one call site, the JIT sees 30 receiver classes there and can't inline any of them. With an inline forEach, each caller has its own copy of the loop, with exactly one lambda body pasted in. Nothing is left for the JIT to guess.

A crossinline lambda leaves two classes behind. Run javap -p on the ModifiersDemoKt$... classes in kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/:

ModifiersDemoKt$runInBackground$1 implements java.lang.Runnable {
  final kotlin.jvm.functions.Function0<kotlin.Unit> $task;   // used when Java calls the compiled body
  public final void run();
}
ModifiersDemoKt$main$$inlined$runInBackground$1 implements java.lang.Runnable {
  public final void run();                                   // main's lambda body is pasted in here
}

The first is the template that the compiled runInBackground method uses when Java (or reflection) calls it: it holds the Function0. The second was generated for the one call site in main, with the lambda's body inside run(). Each inlined call site of a crossinline function gets a class like that, which is one more reason to keep these functions few and small.

Finally, a reified inline function has no callable form at all, because its body makes no sense without a concrete type. Kotlin still writes a method into the class file, but marks it ACC_SYNTHETIC, and javac ignores synthetic methods. That's why Java code can't call filterIsInstance<T>()-style functions.
